questions.title: What is the exact mathematical reason why token-level importance sampling fails in GRPO for long sequences?
questions.question_body: I am trying to understand the authors' claim that GRPO's objective is 'ill-posed'. They argue that because the importance weight $w_{i,t}$ is calculated for a single token $y_{i,t}$ sampled from $	heta_{old}$, it fails to perform proper distribution correction. Could someone explain this intuition using the formal definition of importance sampling provided in Section 3? Why exactly does averaging over a single sample per token lead to high variance accumulation over the sequence length $|y|$?

questions.title: How does the exponent $\frac{1}{|y_i|}$ in GSPO's importance ratio $s_i(\theta)$ affect the interpretation of clipping?
questions.question_body: In Equation 6, GSPO defines the sequence-level importance ratio as $s_i(\theta) = \left( \frac{ \pi_{\theta} (y_i | x) }{ \pi_{\theta_{old}} (y_i | x)} \right)^{\frac{1}{|y_i|}}$. The paper mentions this is done to reduce variance and unify numerical ranges. However, since we clip $s_i(\theta)$ directly in Equation 5, doesn't raising the ratio to a fractional power compress extreme values differently depending on sequence length? How do we know that clipping at a fixed range (e.g., $[1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]$) corresponds to a consistent 'degree of off-policyness' regardless of whether $|y_i|$ is short or long?

questions.title: Is GSPO-token mathematically equivalent to GSPO if advantages are uniform?
questions.question_body: Section 4.3 introduces 'GSPO-token', which looks like a token-level objective but uses sequence-level weights via stop-gradient operations. The text states: 'GSPO-token and GSPO are numerically identical... when we set the advantages of all the tokens in the response $y_i$ to the same value.' If this is true, why bother with the complex stop-gradient formulation ($sg[s_i]$)? Does it offer any practical benefit for multi-turn RL or dynamic masking where advantages might *not* be uniform across tokens?

questions.title: Why does MoE expert-volatility invalidate token-level ratios but not sequence-level ratios?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that in MoE models, changing experts between $	heta$ and $	heta_{old}$ causes massive fluctuations in token-level ratios $w_{i,t}$, breaking GRPO. Yet, they claim sequence-level ratios $s_i$ remain stable because 'the MoE model always maintains its language modeling capability.' Intuitively, if an expert switches for just one critical token in a chain-of-thought, shouldn't that cause a massive drop in total sequence probability $ rac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{old}(y|x)}$? Why is the aggregate sequence likelihood less sensitive to individual expert swaps than the pointwise token likelihood?

questions.title: Does GSPO actually solve the off-policy bias problem or just hide it?
questions.question_body: Standard PPO/GRPO rely on clipping to bound off-policy errors. In GSPO, we clip entire sequences based on their geometric mean likelihood ratio. If a sequence has very low probability under $	heta$ but was sampled from $	heta_{old}$ (highly off-policy), clipping removes it entirely. However, isn't there still a risk that we are systematically ignoring regions of high-reward space simply because they require many small deviations from $	heta_{old}$ (which sum up to a low geometric mean)? Does this make GSPO conservative compared to methods that might accept slightly lower probabilities per token if they yield high rewards?
